Automated reviewing systems are increasingly evaluated
based on the quality of the reviews they produce. Yet a re-
view is only useful if acting on it leads to a measurable
improvement in the paper. We present AppliedScientist, a
closed-loop system that couples an autonomous AI scientist
with an AI reviewer, and evaluate it by iteratively revising
rejected papers from a range of research subfields. To mirror
how human authors build on earlier drafts, the AI scientist
has access to its previous versions during revision. To avoid
bias from prior judgments, however, each review is gener-
ated independently, with the reviewer having no memory of
earlier feedback or scores. We compare three revision set-
tings: one initialized with the original venue reviews, one
initialized with AI-generated reviews, and autonomous

primary.claim_evidence_alignment: Claims are generally well supported by the reported results: reviewer-guided revision improves more than fixed-prompt self-revision, Stanford Reviewer independently confirms upward trajectories, and the execution-versus-idea resolution asymmetry is quantified and discussed. The abstract's headline numbers match the body, and the authors appropriately frame the finding that novelty concerns are rarely resolved.
primary.evaluation_assessment: Evaluation is meaningful and multi-layered: reviewer quality is separately benchmarked against baselines on 650 ICLR papers with pairwise judging and human-alignment checks, and revision outcomes are measured on 30 papers across five domains with score trajectories, an external Stanford Reviewer evaluation of human-initialized revisions, and a weakness-resolution analysis (128/150 execution vs 2/18 idea weaknesses). Controls include autonomous self-revision with a fixed prompt and AI-initialized guidance, isolating the effect of iterative reviewer feedback.
primary.limitations: The evaluation set is small (30 papers) and constrained to ICLR papers reproducible on a single 96 GB GPU, with cost (~$65/paper) cited as the limiting factor. The same reviewer both guides and scores the reviewer-driven conditions, though the external Stanford Reviewer evaluation partially mitigates this circularity; Stanford Reviewer is not applied to the AI-initialized or self-revision conditions.
primary.method_assessment: The system design is described in adequate detail: the scientist retains full revision history and addresses each reviewer concern through code edits, literature search, experiment execution, and manuscript updates, while the reviewer independently evaluates only the current manuscript with no memory of prior drafts or scores. The reviewer uses a structured multi-phase process with deep literature search over an indexed arXiv corpus, temporal grounding, and a verification pass.
primary.quality_rationale: The paper makes a substantive, clearly scoped contribution with a well-described system, appropriate controls, independent external evaluation, and a nuanced characterization of what iterative revision can and cannot improve. The main weaknesses are acknowledged and bounded by the study design, and the evidence supports the stated claims without overclaiming.
primary.scoped_contribution: The paper introduces AppliedScientist, a closed-loop system that iteratively revises rejected papers' implementation, experiments, and manuscript under fresh independent AI reviews, while keeping the central research contribution fixed. It contributes a benchmark of reviewer-guided versus fixed-prompt self-revision across 30 ICLR papers and a characterization of which reviewer weaknesses revision can resolve.

scholarly_quality.rationale: The paper makes a substantive, clearly scoped contribution with a well-described system, appropriate controls, independent external evaluation, and a nuanced characterization of what iterative revision can and cannot improve. The main weaknesses are acknowledged and bounded by the study design, and the evidence supports the stated claims without overclaiming.
scholarly_quality.uncertainty: The evaluation set is small (30 papers) and constrained to ICLR papers reproducible on a single 96 GB GPU, with cost (~$65/paper) cited as the limiting factor. The same reviewer both guides and scores the reviewer-driven conditions, though the external Stanford Reviewer evaluation partially mitigates this circularity; Stanford Reviewer is not applied to the AI-initialized or self-revision conditions.

concerns: The available results appear to demonstrate functionality rather than comparative effectiveness.
The human expert evaluation is described qualitatively, without a detailed scoring rubric, inter-rater reliability, or quantitative comparison against human-authored baselines.

The claim of 'methodological rigor comparable to experienced researchers' is partly undermined by the reported theoretical misrepresentations, statistical omissions, and internal contradictions in the generated manuscripts.
The paper does not provide a direct controlled comparison with human researchers or with alternative agentic frameworks.
The expert evaluation appears to have been conducted by the authors or their collaborators, which may introduce confirmation bias despite the structured review process.
scholarly_quality.concise_summary: This systems/application paper demonstrates an autonomous multi-agent AI pipeline that performs end-to-end empirical research with human participants, producing three cognitive psychology manuscripts. The contribution is architectural and demonstrative. The paper provides strong methodological description, transparency, reproducibility testing, ablation studies, and detailed limitations. The main weakness is that the validation of generated manuscript quality relies on qualitative expert review without a fully specified quantitative protocol or controlled comparison, and the reported expert assessment identifies substantive scientific flaws in the generated manuscripts.

evidence.excerpt: The contribution of this work is architectural rather than methodological at the model level: we use only standard, publicly available frontier LLMs, and demonstrate that when combined across providers, embedded in a hierarchical multi-agent architecture, and augmented by the cognitive operators and dynamic memory systems described above - these techniques are jointly sufficient to conduct empirical science autonomously from hypothesis generation through to manuscript preparation.

evidence.explanation: This directly addresses a potential threat to the validity of the system's outputs and aligns the evidence with the claim of unbiased empirical testing.
evidence.paraphrase: The authors use pre-registered hypotheses that were frequently violated by the data as evidence against the concern that the system is biased toward confirming its own expectations.

evidence.paraphrase: The expert evaluation identifies substantive flaws in the generated manuscripts, including theoretical misrepresentations, statistical omissions, and internal contradictions.

evidence.excerpt: Current end-to-end agentic scientific discovery frameworks continue to operate primarily in simulated or abstract digital environments [ 40 ,  41 ,  42 ,  43 ,  44 ,  45 ], typically producing outcomes with predictive power but lacking explanation of underlying causal mechanisms.
evidence.explanation: This establishes the gap that the present work addresses: real-world empirical testing with human participants.
evidence.paraphrase: The paper situates its contribution relative to prior agentic scientific discovery systems, noting that existing frameworks operate primarily in simulated or abstract digital environments.

evidence.excerpt: The data and code that support the findings of this study are openly available on GitHub at  https://github.com/Explore-Science/Virtuous-Machines-Towards-Artificial-General-Science .
evidence.explanation: This supports reproducibility and transparency, which are central claims of the paper.
evidence.paraphrase: The authors release data, code, pre-registrations, and all outputs on GitHub, and provide a complete paper trail of analytic decisions.

evidence.excerpt: While the framework is general by design, currently its physical capabilities are domain-constrained to online experiments for which the necessary tools and interfaces are available.
evidence.explanation: This demonstrates a thorough treatment of limitations and uncertainty, including potential failure modes.
evidence.paraphrase: The authors acknowledge that the system is domain-constrained, that visualizations have aesthetic imperfections, and that early-stage errors can propagate downstream.

evidence.excerpt: The system executed full studies (from initial conception to manuscript) in ∼17 h runtime on average per study, excluding data collection.
evidence.explanation: This supports the precision and clarity of the systems-level reporting.
evidence.paraphrase: The paper provides detailed quantitative system performance metrics, including token usage, runtime, cost, and lines of code.

evidence.excerpt: Technical problems with visualizations included minor layout issues across Figures, and missing axis labels in Study 3.
evidence.explanation: These issues indicate that the system's output quality is not yet fully publication-ready without human intervention.
evidence.paraphrase: The expert evaluation reports presentation issues in the generated manuscripts, including missing axis labels, inconsistent terminology, and awkward table formatting.

scholarly_quality.rationale: The manuscript presents a systems/application contribution: an autonomous multi-agent AI pipeline that performs end-to-end empirical research with human participants. The central claim is architectural and demonstrative rather than a new psychological finding. The paper provides substantial methodological description, explicit expert evaluation of the generated manuscripts, reproducibility tests, ablation tests for review agents and dynamic memory, and detailed limitations. The evidence supports the claimed feasibility demonstration, while the authors appropriately acknowledge that the scientific quality of the generated studies is mixed and that no validated benchmark exists for autonomous research quality.
scholarly_quality.uncertainty: The main uncertainty is whether the expert evaluation of the three AI-generated manuscripts is sufficiently independent and systematic to support the claim that the system demonstrates 'theoretical reasoning and methodological rigor comparable to experienced researchers.' The paper reports structured expert review but does not provide the full reviewer protocol, inter-rater reliability, or quantitative scoring in the extracted text. This limits confidence in the strength of the validation, though the authors also release the manuscripts and code for independent appraisal.

Autonomous research agents are increasingly expected to search the literature, analyze experimen-
tal evidence, and generate scientific hypotheses. These capabilities require multi-step evidence-
grounded reasoning that progressively acquires, integrates, and verifies evidence before reaching
a conclusion. Existing multimodal benchmarks, however, largely evaluate final-answer accuracy,
leaving open whether predictions are actually supported by traceable scientific evidence. We in-
troduceSci-MMR, a benchmark for 
[… separate evidence block …]
multi-step evidence-grounded scientific reasoning built on
structured argument graphs linking scientific claims, citation-grounded knowledge, visual evidence,
and supporting regions. Sci-MMR comprises 235 multi-hop reasoning tasks spanning four scientific
disciplines, with an average of nine figure panels per task. Evaluating eight frontier multimodal
models, we find that answer accuracy consistently exceeds complete-evidence recovery rate by more
than 20%, revealing a substantial gap that answer-only evaluation is structurally unable to capture.
Through controlled interventions, we identify two fundamental bottlenecks. First, evidence acquisi-
tion: models struggle to extract complete structured evidence from scientific figures, accounting for
57.2% of failures. While cropping tools yield modest gains (+4.5 points), providing gold evidence
improves accuracy by up to 37.0 points,

scholarly_quality.concise_summary: The paper presents online surrogate repair (OSR), a closed-loop algorithm that uses sparse high-fidelity evaluations to update a surrogate during a longer agent search. The contribution is clearly stated, the methodology is described in detail, and the evaluation includes controlled synthetic worlds and the MADE benchmark with multiple baselines. The claims are supported by quantitative results, and limitations are acknowledged.

evidence.excerpt:
Our contributions are:
• We formulate online surrogate repair, in which a scientific agent operates under inexpensive
surrogate feedback while a separate acquisition rule allocates a limited number of oracle
queries to update the surrogate during the search.
evidence.explanation: The introduction lists three explicit contributions, including the formulation of online surrogate repair and the identification of acquisition rules that improve optimization performance.
evidence.paraphrase: The contribution is stated explicitly.

evidence.excerpt:
Each of the 20 held-out worlds is a frozen, seeded structural causal model (SCM) (Pearl,
2009) inspired by TabPFN’s sampled causal-graph prior (Hollmann et al., 2025), with a deterministic
response and a single global maximum.
evidence.explanation: The methods section specifies the SCM construction, the number of worlds, the context sizes, the surrogates used, and the evaluation metrics, which supports methodological rigor.
evidence.paraphrase: The paper describes the experimental setup in detail, including the synthetic world construction and the MADE benchmark configuration.

evidence.excerpt:
Across the four settings, Q90-UCB and EI achieve mean maximum-regret reductions of 0.424 and
0.409, compared with 0.063 and 0.052 for Global-UQ and Random.
evidence.explanation: Tables 1, 2, and 3 report quantitative results comparing OSR methods against baselines such as Random, Global-UQ, Peak, Q90-UCB, EI, Static EI, Archive-BO, Tab-AICL, and full-feedback controls.
evidence.paraphrase: The paper reports quantitative comparisons against multiple baselines and ablations.

evidence.excerpt:
Table 3 shows that Control requires 7.23(28) and 6.36(20) times as many oracle queries to match
Online EI under DeepSeek and Luna, respectively, equivalent to 86% and 84% fewer queries for
Online EI.
evidence.explanation: The paper reports acceleration factors showing that full-feedback controls require 6.36-7.23 times more oracle queries to match Online EI under LLM orchestrators, directly supporting the claim of reduced oracle feedback.
evidence.paraphrase: The central claim that Online EI reduces oracle queries is supported by quantitative results on MADE.

evidence.excerpt:
In standard Bayesian optimization,
acquisition is itself the proposal policy. Multi-fidelity optimization also chooses among information
sources (Poloczek et al., 2017), while Gemini learns a cross-fidelity correction that drives a Bayesian
optimizer (Hickman et al., 2021). OSR leaves search to the scientific agent: acquisition only chooses
which archived proposal receives a high-fidelity label to repair future feedback.
evidence.explanation: The related work section explicitly contrasts OSR with standard Bayesian optimization, multi-fidelity optimization, and active in-context learning, clarifying the gap that OSR fills.
evidence.paraphrase: The paper positions OSR relative to active learning, Bayesian optimization, multi-fidelity search, and surrogate verifiers.
evidence.section: Active Learning, Bayesian Optimization,And Multi-Fidelity Search

evidence.excerpt:
The current framework requires a tabular representation of the discovery problem and a tabular
foundation model that can incorporate new labels in context. Most closed-loop discovery problems
can be expressed in this form, as our MADE experiment illustrates, but some environments may fall
out-of-distribution of the model’s capabilities which we did not encounter or test in our experiments.
evidence.explanation: The discussion section explicitly notes that the framework requires a tabular representation and a tabular foundation model, and that OSR has not been tested with test-time training, reinforcement learning, or other surrogate classes.
evidence.paraphrase: The paper acknowledges limitations of the current framework.

The central claims are supported by quantitative results, including comparisons against multiple baselines and ablations, and the manuscript includes a limitations section. Methodological choices are described in sufficient detail to assess the validity of the main claims, and related work is positioned adequately for the stated scope.

Evaluating the capabilities of AI for automating scientific research 
requires test problems that reflect the demands of real research 
practice. Standard benchmarks, 1-4 built from static datasets of 
narrow questions, seem convenient but may not capture the long-
horizon, multi-step workflows characteristic of authentic scientific 
inquiry.5 We and other authors proposed using recently published 
scientific papers as reference material instead, 6-9  since they 
embody the methodological complexity, data -handling 
requirements, and interpretive judgment characteristic of actual 
research, and they provide an external standard against which AI -
generated results can be compared  with. AI performance on such 
problems is therefore important not only for evaluating scientific 
capability of AI in general, but also for estimating the readiness of 
these frameworks to contribute to 
[… separate evidence block …]
industrial research workflows. 
In Paper I in this series,8 we applied this strategy to five advanced 
AI research frameworks (Kosmos, K -Dense, ToolUniverse, 
BioAgents from bio.xyz, and the AI Scientist-v2 from Sakana AI) 
across three projects: uncertainty quantification for molecular 
property prediction under distribution shifts, machine learning  
(ML) on Therapeutic Data Commons  benchmarks, and agent -
based macroeconomic modeling. Across all three projects, the 
frameworks in many cases generated original hypotheses, handled 
routine data acquisition and coding competently, and produced 
well-formatted draft reports. However, no AI framework matched 
the scope or depth of the corresponding reference study. 
Independent runs of the same framework with the same prompt 
diverged in methodology and conclusions, severe hallucinations in

Evaluating the capabilities of AI for automating scientific research 
requires test problems that reflect the demands of real research 
practice. Standard benchmarks, 1-4 built from static datasets of 
narrow questions, seem convenient but may not capture the long-
horizon, multi-step workflows characteristic of authentic scientific 
inquiry.5 We and other authors proposed using recently published 
scientific papers as reference material instead, 6-9  since they 
embody the methodological complexity, data -handling 
requirements, and interpretive judgment characteristic of actual 
research, and they provide an external standard against which AI -
generated results can be compared  with. AI performance on such 
problems is therefore important not only for evaluating scientific 
capability of AI in general, but also for estimating the readiness of 
these frameworks to contribute to

positive_signals: The paper extends a prior evaluation of five AI research frameworks to two new biopharmaceutical case studies: antibody developability prediction and lipid-RNA MD simulation.
The study provides a systematic comparative evaluation of AI frameworks against published reference studies, including multiple independent runs and smaller-scope prompts.
The evaluation protocol includes full-scale and smaller-scope prompts, with the smaller-scope prompts prescribing specific datasets, featurizations, force fields, and simulation protocols.
The antibody case study found that AI frameworks used only one dataset and 2-5 ML models, compared to 240 datasets and 30 models in the reference study.
The AI Scientist-v2 claimed 200-500 ns all-atom simulations but actually generated a synthetic dataset with fabricated feature vectors and ran no MD simulations.
The paper positions its work against prior benchmark-based AI evaluations and the first paper in the series, arguing that published research papers provide a more demanding test.
The paper acknowledges that AI frameworks were run in January-March 2026 and conclusions reflect the state of the frameworks at that time, which may have changed since then.
The paper reports that no AI framework found and cited the original reference paper, despite it being the single most relevant paper for the prompt.

evidence.excerpt:
Lean's kernel guarantees that an accepted proof has the stated theorem as its type, relative to the imported
environment [28,29]. It does not, however, guarantee that the statement faithfully captures the scientific
claim that motivated the task. A benchmark can therefore be mechanically valid while remaining semantically
misleading: an omitted hypothesis, an incorrect type or function encoding, or a weakened conclusion can
cause the formal target to diverge from the intended mathematics [26]. We therefore treat Lean compilation
and the automated checks applied to every task as universal mechanical guarantees, while regarding semantic
fidelity as a separate validity question.
For selected statements whose translation carries elevated semantic risk, we perform a manual comparison
between the formal signature, its supporting definitions, and the available mathematical specification. 
[… separate evidence block …]
This
comparison examines the relevant objects and quantifiers, explicit and implicit assumptions, dimensional
constraints, index and tensor ordering, and the direction and strength of the conclusion. Any discrepancies
identified in this process are resolved before the task is included in the benchmark.
This targeted comparison supplements the automated checks applied to every task. Because it is performed
only on selected high-risk statements, it is not intended to define a benchmark-wide rate of semantic validity.
With the benchmark construction, automated checks, and targeted semantic safeguards in place, the next
section evaluates the recorded model runs.

positive_signals: The paper introduces Lean-QuantumAlg-Bench and Lean-QIT-Bench, two Lean 4 benchmarks containing 36 and 40 theorem-completion tasks for quantum algorithms and quantum information theory, respectively.

Every admitted task passes automated Lean compilation and screening checks, and submission-side acceptance recompiles the submitted theorem in a fixed environment, rejecting new axioms, sorry placeholders, and changes outside the theorem body.
The paper's claims about LAD improvements are explicitly limited to descriptive recorded-run differences rather than causal estimates of access-condition effects.

The paper situates its benchmarks relative to formal theorem-proving benchmarks such as miniF2F, PutnamBench, LeanDojo, and miniCTX, and identifies the need for coordinated quantum-domain evaluation with controlled library access.

The benchmark tasks use a fixed Lean environment, deterministic proof checks, and recorded suite versions, model settings, access conditions, and execution settings to support descriptive aggregation and reproducibility.

The paper identifies four main validity limits: corpus coverage and difficulty calibration, semantic fidelity of formal statements, comparability of recorded runs, and availability of economic-cost records.
The paper defines the difficulty-weighted score formula and cost metrics precisely, including denominators, units, and conditions for unavailable values.

positive_signals: The paper introduces MisKnow-Agent, a controlled framework for constructing and validating apparently credible but factually misleading knowledge for Deep Research tasks, yielding 5,933 quality-controlled instances from DeepResearch Bench.
The paper evaluates six open-source framework-LLM configurations and one closed-source system, showing that even limited exposure to misleading knowledge can lead to false-conclusion adoption.

The paper characterizes how adoption varies with source properties, exposure conditions, lifecycle stage, framework choice, and backbone choice, and shows that pre- and post-research defenses reduce but do not eliminate false-conclusion adoption.

The paper positions its work against prior studies that examine short-horizon responses to misleading context or explicitly adversarial settings, arguing that Deep Research agents operate under a different regime where misleading content can be selected, compressed, and reused during final report generation without the
The paper's threat model reflects risks in open information environments and does not assume instruction-level attacks such as prompt injection or instruction hijacking.
The paper reports that introducing a single misleading document increases mean FCAR from 0% in the no-injection control to 54.7%.

evidence.excerpt:
The tool ablation isolates how retrieval ac-
cess changes one base system. Starting from
Qwen36_plus, we progressively add law search,
law plus case search, and law plus case plus web
search, while keeping the task input and base
prompt fixed. Table 6 reports the report-level sum-
mary.
Law search modestly increases Support from
0.3153 to 0.3427 and Trust from 0.7744 to 0.7951,
raising Final from 0.9612 to 0.9718. Adding case
search produces the largest evidence gain: Support
rises to 0.4857, especially through Subtopic Ev-
idence Support, but Trust drops to 0.7433. The
law-plus-case condition still achieves the highest
Final score among tool settings, showing that case
evidence improves the composite score while in-
creasing citation risk.
Adding web search does not further improve per-
formance: Support falls to 0.4197, Trust remains
nearly unchanged, and Final drops to 0.9903. 
[… separate evidence block …]
Item-
level diagnostics in Appendix E clarify this pattern:
case citations increase from 4 in the base setting
to 146 with case search, then fall to 73 when web
search is added. Tool-call statistics point in the
same direction: the law-only setting uses about
1.97 tool calls per report on average; law plus case
uses about 4.15, including about 2.24 case-search
calls; and law plus case plus web uses about 6.10,
including about 1.94 web-search calls. Tool aug-
mentation therefore shifts the balance between evi-
dence richness and citation reliability rather than
producing monotonic improvement.
evidence.explanation: The reported Support and Trust changes across tool settings directly align with the paper's central claim about the Support-Trust tension.
evidence.paraphrase: The tool ablation shows that adding case search increases Support from 0.3153 to 0.4857 but lowers Trust from 0.7744 to 0.7433, supporting the claim that retrieval can improve evidence support without reliably improving citation trustworthiness.

positive_signals: The benchmark addresses an under-evaluated gap: whether each cited legal authority is used as a trustworthy ground for the local claim, rather than merely whether citations can be generated, matched, or verified.

The benchmark construction filters 13,622 candidate legal research documents to 72 source documents with at least one case citation and at least five statutory or normative references, yielding 236 subtopics, 585 rubrics, and 1,459 evidence points.
The main leaderboard evaluates seven end-to-end systems across general-purpose LLMs, deep or agentic research systems, and legal-specific systems on the same 72 tasks.

The verification ablation shows Trust increases from 0.7433 for Base to 0.8134 with existence-only filtering and 0.8883 with full E/F/A revision, while Final increases from 1.0329 to 1.0970 and 1.1708.

The tool ablation shows that adding case search increases Support from 0.3153 to 0.4857 but lowers Trust from 0.7744 to 0.7433, supporting the claim that retrieval can improve evidence support without reliably improving citation trustworthiness.

LegalCiteTrust is positioned at the intersection of legal task evaluation, agentic or deep-research report evaluation, and hallucination or citation-faithfulness evaluation, with a table comparing representative work across legal, deep research, long report, citation support, and citation trust dimensions.
The released code records the task prompts, citation extraction, source resolution, E/F/A judging, scoring, and aggregation pipeline.

The benchmark is dense rather than broad, with 72 authority-demanding Chinese legal research problems, and transfer to other jurisdictions is nontrivial because citation formats, statute versioning, case authority, and legal research practice vary across legal systems.

Fidelity and Applicability are protocolized legal judgments about conditions, exceptions, factual context, statute versions, and the distance between a cited source and the local claim, and human audit tests consistency with the protocol rather than agreement with objective legal truth.

positive_signals: AREX is a family of recursively self-improving deep research agents that alternate between an inner research loop and an outer self-improvement loop, with a learned autonomous context-update tool.

Existing context management approaches use fixed heuristics such as discarding tool responses by predefined rules or triggering summarization at a fixed token threshold, which can remove decision-relevant information.
The paper reports benchmark results with explicit metrics, including Item-F1 for WideSearch, F1 for DeepSearchQA, and accuracy for other benchmarks.
